doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

chapter: Jazz in the academy and critics
title: Sacred and secular music, and teaching students to cross-reference
summary: Jazz and gospel share technique; he tells students to check sources, citing a Kenny G Charlie Parker nickname claim.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: a lot of jazz musicians in terms of the academic community would always say oh those jazz musicians play out of tune. Because they don’t recognize it’s coming from a different source. And it’s not going to have that kind of thing because it’s not that type of music in its purest form. So you can’t use that as a barometer to negate or whatever. It’s all music, but all musics have their particular parameters that codify what that music is. So in understanding — and there’s also the argument in the African-American community about this because a lot of them would like try to put jazz down and say oh that’s the Devil’s music as opposed to the spirituals which led to the Gospels. And it’s all a matter — those same musical techniques are utilized. When you hear Aretha Franklin sing “Amazing Grace,” and when she sings the blues she’s still using the same technique. So it’s a question of the sacred text versus the secular text. And that’s the only difference. Thomas E. Dorsey, who is considered the father of Gospel music, was a jazz piano player. He played jazz. And then he found a niche of moving over into that particular arena. And the Gospels, people tend to forget that the Gospels grew out of the spirituals. And a lot of those things came out of the old African chants and things like that. So there’s that tie. You can’t chop it off and say that it started now. No, no. We all are the sum of many parts — S-U-M — and we are also a part of a tradition and a legacy. But there are a lot of people who are not being taught that and the insight into understanding how important it is if you truly want to be a person of substance you must go back and you must — I used to tell my students all the time at Rutgers — I was there for 28 years — and I told them I said look just don’t take everything I say as being total Gospel. I want you to cross reference what I am telling you. Because that’s what I’ve done in arriving at the conclusions that I have. And it’s important for you so that you are truly ingrained with feeling that you are confident in taking the stance in the posture you have. You’re entitled to your own ideas and your feelings about a lot of things. But make sure that your points of view are responsible and well thought out and well researched. And that way you don’t find yourself caught in the cross about all these things. If somebody says, “Well how do you know that?” Well going back you can begin to tie it in. So you’re just not making wild assumptions. Case in point there’s a thing in the new Jazz Times where Gary Giddins is talking about Kenny G. And I must check with Gary to find out if this is really true but supposedly in an interview with Ted Pankin, who is with WKCR FM in New York, the Columbia University jazz radio station, they feature a lot of jazz because Phil Schaap is there. Kenny G supposedly attributes the fact that Charlie Parker got his nickname Bird because he had something happen with his reeds and it sounded like he was chirping. Now I hope — I didn’t mean to mess up my interview, it was Monk talking about Kenny G.
